javascript: JavaScript JavaScript is a programming language whose core semantics are standardized as ECMAScript; browsers and server runtimes supply additional APIs around that language. Language, engine and runtime The language defines values, expressions, objects, functions and execution rules. An engine implements these rules. A runtime combines an engine with host facilities: a browser exposes the DOM, while Node.js exposes server-oriented APIs. A browser API is not automatically part of ECMAScript. JavaScript lets developers describe behavior rather than encode every instruction for a specific processor. Functions create execution contexts represented on the call stack. Work in a single agent executes one job at a time; host facilities coordinate timers, network completion and other asynchronous work. A practical example The synchronous messages print before the promise reaction. The reaction runs later at a microtask checkpoint; the promise does not create a new operating-system thread. See the event loop for the scheduling mechanism. Boundaries and common mistakes Long synchronous work can block browser interaction even inside an async function. Awaiting a value permits continuation scheduling; it does not move computation to another core. Web Workers supply a separate execution context for appropriate browser computation. Avoid executing strings received from users. Validate external values at a trust boundary and use safe document APIs when rendering them. Dynamic typing makes runtime checks particularly important. Learning progression First practice variables, functions, arrays and object identity. Then trace a function call and a promise reaction by hand. Assessment: explain which behavior comes from ECMAScript and which comes from the host. Continue with concurrency before comparing browser and server scheduling. event-loop: Event loop An event loop coordinates scheduled work in a host environment. In a browser, it selects tasks, runs microtask checkpoints and participates in deciding when rendering can occur. Why it exists A browser must respond to input, network completion and timers while running application code. These activities become ready at different times. The event loop supplies scheduling rules that allow JavaScript to react to them without requiring every application to manage an operating-system thread for each activity. “JavaScript is single-threaded” is useful only with a scope: one agent executes one job at a time. A browser has other processes and threads, and Web Workers execute separately. Tasks, microtasks and rendering A task is scheduled host work, such as a timer callback or an input event dispatch. A microtask is work processed at defined checkpoints, including promise reactions and callbacks scheduled with queueMicrotask . A simplified browser sequence is: 1. Select a runnable task from the available task sources. 2. Execute its JavaScript; nested function calls use the call stack. 3. At the appropriate checkpoint, drain queued microtasks, including microtasks added by other microtasks. 4. When a rendering opportunity is due, update the rendering. 5. Repeat. There is not one universal FIFO “callback queue” for all browser activity. Task sources, rendering opportunities and host rules matter. Rendering is not guaranteed after every task. Predict an execution order For this isolated browser example, the output is A, B, microtask, promise, timer. Microtasks are enqueued in the order shown. A zero timer delay makes a timer eligible after its minimum waiting rules; it is not an instruction to interrupt currently executing JavaScript. What async does not promise An async function begins executing synchronously until it reaches a suspension point. A large loop before that point still blocks its agent. Wrapping CPU-heavy code in a promise does not create parallelism. Move suitable computation to a worker or split it into bounded units that yield appropriately. Node.js also uses event-loop scheduling but has different host APIs and phases. Do not transfer every browser ordering claim to Node. Runtime versions and the kind of callback being executed can affect ordering examples. Debugging a frozen page Use a performance recording to find long tasks, then inspect the call tree. A long call stack indicates synchronous work. Repeated microtasks can also starve tasks and rendering even when each callback is short. Measure the actual user-visible delay. Distinguish slow network completion, expensive JavaScript and layout/paint work. An empty task queue is not proof that an application is responsive if its microtasks never finish. Exercise and assessment Run the example in browser DevTools. Add a microtask inside the first microtask and predict its position before executing. Next compare a synchronous calculation with a worker-based version. Record interaction latency and explain the serialization overhead. A successful explanation distinguishes task readiness, microtask checkpoints and rendering opportunities; it does not describe promises as background threads. Frontend, performance and runtime engineers use this model to diagnose interaction stalls and race-like ordering bugs. References and verification These sources are provided for claim review. call-stack: Call stack A call stack records active function invocations so execution can return to the caller when a function finishes. How calls nest When one function calls another, the runtime tracks the new invocation above its caller. Returning removes the active invocation and resumes the caller. A stack therefore follows last-in, first-out order. Actual engine representation may be optimized; the conceptual call chain remains useful. While square is active, its callers have not finished. A debugger can show local values at each frame. Stack versus trace A stack is runtime state. A stack trace is a report of a call chain, often captured when an error occurs. Async continuations may be presented with reconstructed async context; a displayed trace is not always a literal snapshot of one physical stack. The event loop starts later jobs after earlier synchronous execution yields. A timer does not sit on the stack until it expires. Problems and trade-offs Recursion creates repeated calls and can exhaust a finite stack. A missing termination case is a common cause. Replacing recursion with iteration can help, but first establish whether depth is expected or caused by a logic error. Error reports can reveal internal paths or secrets in arguments; expose a safe user message while retaining appropriately protected diagnostic context. Practice Set a breakpoint in square , inspect each caller, and step out. Then build a recursive sum with a clear base case. Assessment: explain why the stack grows and when it shrinks. Continue with debugging and distinguish invocation state from the shared memory of threads. References and verification These sources are provided for claim review. web-workers: Web Workers Web Workers allow scripts to run in a worker execution environment separate from the page's main execution environment. Why use a worker? A page that calculates a large result synchronously can delay input and rendering. A worker lets suitable computation proceed separately while the page remains available. It cannot directly manipulate the page's DOM; it exchanges messages with the page instead. Messages normally use structured cloning. Transferable buffers can transfer ownership without copying their contents. Shared memory is a separate mechanism with additional synchronization and deployment requirements. Cost and failure handling Starting workers and sending large data structures costs time and memory. A tiny calculation may be slower in a worker. Handle worker errors, bound the size of incoming messages and terminate workers when their lifetime ends. An untrusted message is still external input. Validate message structure and define a small protocol rather than accepting arbitrary executable code. Learning exercise Build a worker that summarizes an array and show a loading state while it runs. Add a request identifier so late responses cannot overwrite newer results. Measure interaction responsiveness as well as total duration. Assessment: distinguish concurrency, parallelism and message-copying cost. Server-side JavaScript uses the related but different worker-thread API in Node.js. References and verification These sources are provided for claim review. nodejs: Node.js Node.js is a JavaScript runtime that combines a JavaScript engine with server and operating-system APIs, including asynchronous I/O and worker-thread facilities. Runtime rather than language JavaScript is the language. Node.js supplies APIs for networking, files, processes and other host activities. Its event loop and libuv integration coordinate many asynchronous operations; this does not mean every operation runs on the same thread or that every asynchronous API uses a background thread. A server can wait for many I/O operations while its JavaScript agent processes callbacks. CPU-heavy JavaScript still consumes that agent's execution time. Example: a small HTTP server The server exposes HTTP behavior. It is not a production authentication or routing layer. Choosing an execution mechanism Use asynchronous I/O APIs for waiting on supported I/O. Consider worker threads for sustained CPU work, with bounded worker counts and message sizes. Separate processes provide a stronger memory boundary but have different communication costs. A blocked event loop can delay unrelated requests. Timeouts, input limits and cancellation are therefore reliability and security controls, not just performance tuning. Practice Compare a slow asynchronous file operation with a deliberately CPU-heavy calculation while making another request. Observe response delays. Assessment: explain why async I/O helps the first case while merely labeling the calculation async does not help the second. Continue with the event loop, testing and observability. dom: Document Object Model The DOM represents a document as objects and nodes with interfaces that programs can inspect and modify. Document, tree and display HTML source is parsed into a document tree. Elements, text and other nodes become accessible through APIs. The DOM is not the same thing as the original source text or the pixels on screen: scripts can change nodes, and style/layout/painting determine their visual presentation. JavaScript commonly uses the DOM, but the DOM is an API model rather than part of the JavaScript language. Safe content insertion Using textContent treats the value as text. Interpreting untrusted strings as HTML can introduce script injection; input validation alone does not replace correct output handling. Events and performance Event listeners respond to user or programmatic events. Dispatch can invoke several listeners according to event propagation rules. Frequent interleaved layout reads and writes may force expensive rendering work. Workers cannot directly edit the page DOM. They can calculate a result and send it to the page, which applies an update. Practice Create a list, append items with element APIs and handle clicks with one listener on its container. Use a debugger to inspect the clicked node and propagation. Assessment: explain why a DOM mutation does not mean the browser has already painted a frame. Continue with the event loop and Web Workers. processes: Processes A process is an operating-system execution environment that groups resources such as an address space, open handles and one or more threads. Isolation and execution A program is executable code; a process is a running instance with resources and state. Two processes can run the same program while retaining different memory and credentials. Their threads perform the actual scheduled execution. Process boundaries help isolate failures and enforce access checks. They are not a complete security guarantee: privileges, shared resources and the operating system's isolation mechanisms still matter. Communication Processes can exchange data through pipes, sockets, shared memory and other inter-process communication mechanisms. Sending a serialized message creates an explicit interface; sharing memory demands agreement about layout and synchronization. A browser may use multiple processes for sites, rendering or supporting services. Exact arrangements vary by browser and configuration. Trade-offs and diagnosis More processes can improve isolation but increase memory overhead and communication costs. A process may be alive while doing no useful work, waiting on I/O or deadlocked. During debugging, inspect CPU usage, memory, open resources and wait state separately. Do not infer CPU parallelism simply from a count of processes. Exercise Run two independent instances of a small program. Record their process identifiers, change state in one and check whether the other changes. Then connect them with a simple message protocol. Assessment: identify which state is private and which is intentionally shared. Next compare concurrency and parallelism. References and verification These sources are provided for claim review. threads: Software threads A software thread is an execution sequence that an operating system or runtime can schedule, usually sharing a process's address space with other threads in that process. Shared resources, separate execution state Threads within a process commonly share heap memory and open resources. Each thread has its own execution state, including a stack and registers. Exact ownership rules depend on the platform. A software thread is not a CPU core. A hardware thread is a processor execution context; an operating system can schedule many software threads over a smaller number of hardware execution contexts. Example: a shared counter Two threads can both read the same counter value before either writes the incremented value. One update may be lost. Protect the operation with an appropriate synchronization primitive or avoid sharing the mutable counter. Atomic access to one value does not automatically make a multi-step business operation atomic. Costs and risks Threads can support parallelism on available hardware, but context switching, contention and cache effects can limit gains. Locks can introduce deadlocks when threads acquire resources in inconsistent orders. Memory safety and synchronization bugs can become security problems when corrupted state controls access or resource ownership. Practice Describe a two-thread lost-update interleaving on paper, then design a message-passing alternative. Assessment: state which data is shared, which operations need coordination and how a thread stops safely. Study concurrency before assuming additional threads improve throughput. concurrency: Concurrency Concurrency is the organization of multiple activities whose lifetimes overlap, allowing each to make progress without requiring simultaneous execution. Overlap is the key A service can begin several network requests and handle each result when it arrives. On a single CPU execution context, work may be interleaved. This is concurrent even if only one instruction stream runs at a time. Parallelism specifically involves simultaneous work. Concurrency exists because many tasks spend time waiting for I/O, other services or resources. An event loop, threads and multiple processes are different mechanisms for managing it. Ordering still matters Suppose a user searches for “tcp” and then “tls”. The first request may finish last. If the UI blindly accepts every response, it can display obsolete results. Associate results with a request identifier or cancel obsolete work where supported. This is an ordering bug even without shared-memory threads. Design constraints Bound the number of outstanding operations so queues cannot grow indefinitely. Define timeouts, cancellation and cleanup. Shared mutable resources need synchronization or ownership rules; asynchronous code does not remove these obligations. Practice Draw a timeline for three overlapping requests, including one failure and one cancellation. Specify which results the user should see. Assessment: explain the difference between a completed task, an abandoned caller and a stopped underlying operation. Continue with threads, testing and observability. parallelism: Parallelism Parallelism means performing multiple pieces of work at the same time using multiple execution resources. When it helps Independent chunks of a computation can run on separate cores, workers or machines. A large image-processing task may split the image into regions, process regions concurrently on available resources, then combine the output. Concurrency describes overlapping activities; parallelism describes simultaneous execution. A concurrent program can run on one core, and a parallel program still needs coordination. Limits to speedup Splitting and combining work costs time. Serial portions, memory bandwidth, communication and synchronization limit the gain. Doubling the worker count does not imply halving elapsed time. A worker is a software abstraction; actual simultaneous execution depends on hardware availability and scheduling. Excessive workers can worsen performance through contention. Correctness and security Parallel tasks must agree on ownership of input and output. Unsynchronized writes can corrupt results. Cancellation should stop unnecessary work and release resources rather than leave an unbounded backlog. Exercise Choose a pure calculation that can be partitioned. Compare one worker with two and four, recording both duration and memory use. Explain why small inputs may become slower. Assessment: identify the serial fraction and data-transfer overhead. computer-networks: Computer networks A computer network connects devices so they can exchange information using agreed communication rules called protocols. Layers solve different problems A physical medium carries signals. A link technology such as Ethernet delivers frames on a link. IP carries packets across networks. A transport such as TCP provides an application-facing communication service. HTTP defines application messages. Layer models are explanatory tools, not a requirement that every real implementation fit perfectly into a diagram. Distinguish the OSI reference model from the deployed Internet protocol suite. Follow one request A client resolves a name using DNS, chooses an IP address and contacts an application endpoint identified partly by a port. Routers forward traffic between networks; application authorization remains a separate responsibility. Common problems A successful Wi-Fi connection proves neither Internet connectivity nor access to a particular service. Diagnose link state, address configuration, name resolution, transport reachability and application response separately. A firewall can permit one protocol and block another. Capture only traffic you own or are authorized to inspect; traces can contain sensitive information. Practice Diagram the route from your browser to a local test server. Identify the address, port and application protocol at each endpoint. Assessment: distinguish a DNS failure from a TCP refusal and an HTTP error. Continue with TLS to understand how traffic can be protected across untrusted links. References and verification These sources are provided for claim review. ip-address: IP address An IP address identifies an interface or a set of interfaces for Internet Protocol delivery within an addressing and routing context. Address rather than identity IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses. An address can change over time, and a device can have several addresses. It is not a reliable permanent identifier for a person or application. A network prefix determines a block of addresses. Routing uses prefixes to select where packets should go. A private address may be useful inside one network while being reused independently elsewhere. Names, addresses and services DNS can return address records for a name. An application then uses a transport protocol and port to contact a service. One name can map to several addresses, and many names can point to the same address. Network address translation can rewrite addressing information. The public address observed by a server may represent many clients. Troubleshooting and boundaries Check the interface, prefix, gateway and intended address family. A reachable IPv4 endpoint does not establish that IPv6 works. An address alone proves neither service health nor authorization. Avoid treating IP allowlists as a substitute for authenticating a user. Addresses can be shared, reassigned or hidden behind proxies. Exercise Inspect your own interface configuration. Label loopback, local network and externally routed addresses where present. Resolve a test domain and note the address families returned. Assessment: explain why changing an IP address does not automatically change a service's name or credentials. Next study TCP. References and verification These sources are provided for claim review. dns: Domain Name System DNS is a distributed hierarchical naming system that publishes resource records under domain names, including records used to locate Internet services. Simple explanation A memorable name such as example.com is not itself an IP address. DNS lets software ask for information associated with that name. Address lookup is one use; mail routing, aliases and other data are also represented by DNS records. DNS exists so names can be administered in a distributed way while service addresses can change without requiring users to memorize new addresses. The hierarchy and its participants The DNS namespace is a tree rooted at the root zone. Delegation assigns authority for parts of the tree to other name servers. | Participant | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Stub resolver | Sends a client's lookup request to a resolver | | Recursive resolver | Obtains the requested answer or an appropriate failure | | Authoritative server | Answers from the zones it serves | | Cache | Retains records for their permitted lifetime | A recursive resolver may already have the answer. On a cache miss, it can follow referrals from root to top-level domain to the authoritative servers for the relevant zone. Actual lookup paths depend on cached delegations and configuration. Records and caching An A record contains an IPv4 address; AAAA contains an IPv6 address. CNAME creates an alias to another name. MX identifies mail exchangers, and NS identifies name servers. The record type is part of the question; DNS is not a single undifferentiated name-to-number table. A time to live (TTL) limits how long a cached record may be reused under normal rules. Changing an authoritative record does not instantly invalidate all existing caches. Lowering a TTL after a stale record has already been cached cannot retroactively shorten that cache's original lifetime. A practical investigation On a system with the appropriate tool, inspect a domain you control or a public documentation domain: Record the resolver used, response type and returned values. Tool behavior and output vary by operating system. Compare the authoritative configuration separately if you administer the zone. When debugging a local application, confirm whether a hosts-file entry, browser cache or local resolver configuration affects the result. “It works by IP” is evidence about naming, but it is not a complete test of an HTTPS service because certificate identity and virtual-host routing still use names. Failure and security A name that does not exist differs from an existing name without the requested record type. A timeout differs from a negative response. A server failure can reflect upstream resolution or configuration problems. DNSSEC supplies data-origin authentication and integrity for signed DNS data; it does not encrypt queries. Encrypted resolver transports address different privacy and transport concerns. Neither proves that an application reached through a name is trustworthy. Do not log unnecessary user query histories. Protect registrar and zone-management access because DNS changes can redirect services. Learning progression Start with computer networks and addressing. Then explain a warm-cache and cold-cache lookup, identify the authoritative party, and diagnose one intentionally misspelled name. Assessment: distinguish name resolution from TCP connection setup and HTTPS identity verification. Network, backend, cloud and reliability engineers use these distinctions when debugging outages. ports: Transport ports and sockets A transport port is a numbered identifier used with an address and transport protocol to distinguish communication endpoints; a socket is an operating-system or runtime abstraction for network communication. Which service receives the data? An IP address routes traffic toward an interface. A TCP or UDP port helps deliver that traffic to the appropriate transport endpoint. TCP port 443 and UDP port 443 belong to different transport namespaces. A TCP connection is commonly identified using the source and destination addresses and ports, together with the transport protocol. A server can serve many clients on one listening port because their connection endpoints differ. Example A development server listening on 127.0.0.1:3000 is reachable through loopback on that machine. Binding to all interfaces can make it reachable from other networks, depending on firewall and routing rules. Changing the port does not provide authentication. Debugging “Connection refused” often indicates that the destination actively rejected the connection, such as when no server is listening. A timeout can have several causes, including packet loss or filtering. Neither message by itself establishes the complete root cause. Check the bind address, protocol, listening process and firewall policy before changing application code. Practice Run a local Node.js test server and request it on the correct and incorrect ports. Observe the difference between a connection error and an HTTP 404. Assessment: explain why a port identifies an endpoint rather than proving which application is actually running there. tcp: Transmission Control Protocol TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte-stream service between endpoints over IP, with connection management, retransmission, flow control and congestion control. What the application receives TCP delivers a stream of bytes. It does not preserve application message boundaries. One write can arrive through several reads, or several writes can be returned in one read. Applications must define framing through lengths, delimiters or another protocol. TCP uses sequence numbers and acknowledgments to track byte delivery. Lost data can be retransmitted. Flow control protects the receiver's available capacity, while congestion control limits pressure on the network. A practical consequence A receiver that expects one JSON object per socket read can fail when messages are split or combined. A length-prefixed protocol first reads a fixed-size length field, then accumulates exactly that many payload bytes. HTTP defines its own message semantics and framing; it should not be replaced by assumptions about packet sizes. Reliability has limits A delivered byte stream does not prove that a remote business operation committed. A client can lose the connection after a server processed a request but before receiving confirmation. Retry design therefore needs application-level idempotency. TCP does not encrypt content or authenticate a server's real-world identity. TLS can supply transport protection above it for appropriate applications. Exercise Explain how a receiver should handle partial data and connection closure. Sketch a request that might be processed twice after a timeout. Assessment: separate network delivery from application success. Prerequisites are IP addressing and ports. References and verification These sources are provided for claim review. http: Hypertext Transfer Protocol HTTP is an application-level protocol that defines request and response semantics for interacting with resources and exchanging representations. Messages and representations A request identifies a target and method, along with fields and sometimes content. A response includes a status and fields, with content where appropriate. A server can return HTML, JSON, images, video or other representations. HTTP is the communication protocol; HTML and JSON are content formats. This is illustrative HTTP/1.1 message syntax. Later HTTP versions encode messages differently while retaining much of the same semantics. Method and status meaning GET requests a representation and is defined as safe. POST performs resource-specific processing. A 200 response differs from a 404 or 500, but the application must still interpret the body according to its contract. A successful status is not a guarantee that returned data is correct. A Content-Type field describes the representation. Content can be binary, which explains why DevTools sometimes displays raw bytes instead of readable text. Reliability and security Retry decisions depend on method semantics and application design. Caches must respect freshness and variation rules. Sensitive data should not be placed in URLs casually because URLs are often logged. Use HTTPS for protected communication and enforce authorization on the server. The transport does not decide which records a caller may access. Practice Inspect one document request and one image request in browser DevTools. Compare method, status, fields and response body. https: HTTPS HTTPS is HTTP communication secured using TLS, providing confidentiality and integrity in transit and authenticated server identity when certificate validation succeeds. What protection means HTTP supplies application semantics. TLS supplies a protected channel and certificate-based identity checks in typical web use. The client checks that the presented certificate is valid for the requested name and chains to a trusted authority under its policy. Different HTTP versions use different transport arrangements. Avoid equating all HTTPS connections with one fixed TCP handshake diagram; HTTP/3 uses QUIC with TLS integrated into its security design. What HTTPS cannot establish A correctly encrypted connection can still lead to a malicious website. HTTPS does not validate business claims, eliminate application vulnerabilities or replace authentication and authorization. TLS often terminates at a reverse proxy. Protection between that proxy and the application requires its own deployment decisions. Troubleshooting A certificate-name mismatch differs from an expired certificate or an untrusted issuer. Diagnose the exact validation failure. Disabling verification hides the symptom while removing an important identity check. Mixed-content rules can also affect pages that try to load insecure subresources. Exercise Inspect the certificate information of a known documentation website in the browser. Identify the requested name and certificate subject names. Assessment: explain why connecting to a server by its raw IP address may fail identity validation even when DNS was the original problem. tls: Transport Layer Security TLS is a cryptographic protocol family that establishes protected communication channels with confidentiality, integrity and peer authentication according to the selected configuration. Handshake and protected data During a TLS handshake, peers negotiate supported parameters and establish shared traffic secrets. In common web deployments, the server presents a certificate and proves possession of its private key. Application data is then protected using authenticated encryption. Certificate validation, protocol negotiation and key exchange solve different problems. Encryption without correct identity validation can protect a connection to the wrong peer. Application example A browser uses TLS as part of HTTPS. An MQTT deployment can also use TLS. The application protocol still defines its own requests, permissions and delivery behavior. “SSL” is often used informally for TLS, but historical SSL protocols are not interchangeable with modern TLS versions. Failure and operational trade-offs Certificate renewal, trust-store management and key protection are operational responsibilities. A private key leak can compromise identity even if the implementation uses strong algorithms. TLS protects data in transit, not data already available to either endpoint. Logs and stored records still need appropriate handling. Practice Draw a boundary around the channel TLS protects in a client → proxy → application deployment. Identify who holds certificates and where plaintext becomes available. Assessment: distinguish confidentiality, integrity and authentication, and explain why TLS alone does not authorize a user to read another user's records. usb: Universal Serial Bus USB is a family of standards for connecting hosts and peripherals, defining communication, device discovery and associated electrical and power behavior. Why it exists A computer needs a consistent way to discover peripherals and exchange data with them. USB provides a host-controlled communication architecture and standardized device classes. A compatible keyboard can work through an existing class driver instead of requiring a separate application for every model. USB is not one connector shape. Connector type, data capability, power capability and supported protocol versions are separate properties. A USB-C connector alone does not establish a cable's speed or every feature a port supports. Host, device and controller A host manages the bus and schedules communication. A device exposes capabilities to the host. A hub expands downstream connectivity. Controllers implement the relevant host or device functions in hardware and software. A microcontroller needs appropriate hardware and firmware support to act as a USB device. An adapter with a USB connector is not necessarily programmable as any desired device class. Enumeration and descriptors When a device attaches, the host performs enumeration. It obtains structured descriptors, assigns an address and selects an appropriate configuration. Descriptors describe capabilities such as interfaces and endpoints. The operating system matches interfaces with suitable drivers. An interface groups a function. An endpoint is a logical data source or sink on the device. A single physical device can expose several interfaces, such as serial communication and an input device. This is why physical appearance is not a reliable description of USB behavior. Transfers and classes USB defines control, bulk, interrupt and isochronous transfer types with different scheduling and delivery properties. USB “interrupt transfer” does not mean the peripheral arbitrarily interrupts the host outside the USB scheduling model. USB HID defines reports and descriptors for human-interface devices. Mass Storage defines another class of behavior. A keyboard and a storage drive can share a connector while presenting very different interfaces. Practical investigation Connect a trusted peripheral you own and inspect it through your operating system's device information tools. Record the manufacturer/model, exposed interfaces and loaded drivers. Disconnect and reconnect it; note the difference between physical attachment, successful enumeration and application-level function. For deeper analysis, distinguish software capture from a dedicated hardware protocol analyzer. A software trace does not necessarily show every electrical event on the bus. Security and reliability Descriptors are declarations, not proof that a peripheral is trustworthy. USB security includes unwanted input, unexpected network interfaces, vulnerable drivers, removable-media risks and physical electrical hazards. Scanning files alone cannot assess all these risks. A device that repeatedly disconnects may have a cable, power, signal-integrity, firmware or driver problem. Diagnose the layer before replacing code. A charge-only cable can supply power while providing no usable data path. Exercise and progression First learn basic computer architecture and firmware. Then trace the lifecycle: attach → enumerate → bind driver → exchange class-specific data. Assessment: explain why “the computer sees the USB device” does not guarantee the application can use it. embedded-systems: Embedded systems An embedded system combines computing hardware and software within a product or process to perform defined functions, often under timing, power or resource constraints. Choosing an interface requires electrical compatibility and timing knowledge, not just matching connector labels. A concrete sensor logger Consider a temperature logger: 1. Initialize power-dependent hardware and the sensor interface. 2. Read a measurement at a defined interval. 3. Validate the returned value and communication status. 4. Timestamp and buffer the reading. 5. Store it locally or transmit it, for example through MQTT. 6. Handle disconnected sensors, full buffers and unavailable networks. A missing measurement should not silently become a valid zero. A network outage should not indefinitely block a time-critical control loop. authorization: Authorization Authorization determines whether a subject may perform a requested action on a resource under the current policy and context. Subject, action and resource Authentication may identify a user. Authorization then asks whether that user can read a particular note, update an inventory record or administer settings. Policies can use roles, attributes, relationships and resource ownership. A role name alone is not a complete universal access model. A record-level example A signed-in user requests /notes/123 . The server must check whether note 123 belongs to the user or is shared with them. Hiding the link in the UI does not protect the route. A syntactically valid identifier is not evidence of access. Enforce checks at the server-side operation boundary and apply least privilege. Deny by default when policy is missing or uncertain. Common failures Checking only “is logged in,” trusting a client-supplied owner ID or protecting list pages but not direct record routes can expose data. Import/export and background-job paths also need policy enforcement. Caching a decision can become unsafe when ownership or permissions change; define invalidation and re-check critical operations. Practice Create an access matrix for owner, shared reader and unrelated user. Test read, edit, delete and export separately. Assessment: demonstrate that changing an identifier does not bypass the policy. Continue with testing, input validation and audit-oriented observability. git: Git Git is a distributed version-control system that records project snapshots and their history, supporting local work and collaboration through repositories and references. Working tree, index and history The working tree contains checked-out files. The index stages content for the next commit. A commit records a snapshot with parent history and metadata. Branches are movable references to commits, not separate physical folders by definition. GitHub is a hosting and collaboration service; it is not the Git version-control mechanism itself. A deliberate change These commands illustrate review before committing. Stage only the intended changes and inspect them. A commit does not automatically publish anything to a remote service. Collaboration and recovery Merging combines histories; conflicts require understanding the intended behavior, not choosing one entire file blindly. Rewriting published history changes commit identities and can disrupt collaborators. A repository is not a backup for untracked local files or external databases. Credentials committed accidentally can remain in history even after deletion from the latest version. Practice Make two small commits on a practice branch and inspect their difference. Introduce a harmless conflict and resolve it with a behavioral explanation. Assessment: distinguish staged, committed and pushed changes. Continue with CI/CD and software engineering. testing: Software testing Software testing evaluates behavior using planned inputs, observations and expected outcomes to reveal defects and provide evidence about requirements. Different scopes answer different questions A unit test isolates a small behavior. An integration test checks cooperating components, such as an API and persistence. An end-to-end test exercises a user-visible workflow through a larger system. These labels vary across teams; state the actual boundary and dependencies of each test. Example: saving a note A meaningful test creates a note, reloads the application and checks that its content remains. A test that only checks the save function was called does not prove persistence. Failure cases include invalid input, missing permissions, unavailable storage and duplicate requests. Input validation and authorization each need different test cases. Limits and reliability Passing tests are evidence for the cases exercised, not proof of universal correctness. Brittle tests can fail after harmless presentation changes; excessive mocking can hide broken integration. Make test data deterministic and isolate it from real personal data. Restore or clean up test-created records without touching unrelated user work. Practice Write one acceptance criterion, a successful example and a boundary or failure case. Explain what defect each test could detect. Assessment: demonstrate that an intentional behavior regression causes a useful failure. Continue with debugging to investigate failures and CI/CD to run important checks consistently. References and verification These sources are provided for claim review. debugging: Debugging Debugging is the evidence-driven process of locating, explaining and correcting the causes of unexpected system behavior. Reproduce, observe, explain Start with expected versus actual behavior, the environment and a minimal reproduction. Gather evidence, form a hypothesis, change one relevant variable and compare the result. A symptom disappearing after a restart does not establish its cause. Breakpoints and the call stack reveal execution state. Network traces reveal requests and timing. Hardware instruments reveal signals software logs may not capture. Example: missing sensor data Distinguish a sensor that never responds, a parser rejecting bytes, a queue dropping records and a UI failing to display them. Each hypothesis predicts different evidence. For a web page, a successful HTTP response does not prove that its contents were valid or rendered correctly. Reliable fixes Preserve the failing evidence, apply the smallest justified correction and verify the original case plus a nearby regression case. Record why the fix addresses the mechanism. Redact secrets from logs and screenshots. Avoid repeatedly modifying production data while guessing. Practice Create a troubleshooting record with reproduction steps, observations, hypotheses, rejected explanations and final validation. Assessment: another person should be able to follow the reasoning and reproduce the result. Continue with testing, observability and concurrency for timing-related failures. ci-cd: Continuous integration and delivery Continuous integration frequently integrates changes with automated checks; continuous delivery keeps changes releasable, while continuous deployment automatically releases eligible changes under defined policy. Pipeline responsibilities A typical pipeline checks out an exact revision, installs declared dependencies, runs selected tests and builds an artifact. A delivery stage promotes that artifact to an environment. Continuous delivery and continuous deployment are related practices with different release decisions. A green pipeline should have a clear meaning rather than imply that every possible risk was tested. Example A documentation platform can validate content IDs, test relationship navigation, type-check its code and build static assets on each proposed change. A deployment then uses the validated revision. Use Git history to connect a release with its source and checks. Security and failure handling Build scripts execute code. Limit credentials, review third-party actions and avoid exposing deployment secrets to untrusted contributions. Pin or constrain dependencies according to the project's update policy. Define what happens when deployment partially fails. Rollback may require handling database or content-format compatibility, not just replacing application files. Practice Write a pipeline diagram listing trigger, inputs, checks, artifact and release gate. Identify which failures stop delivery. Assessment: explain how to reproduce the build and how to trace a deployed artifact to a commit. Continue with testing and observability. observability: Observability Observability is the ability to investigate a system's internal behavior through the evidence it exposes, commonly including logs, metrics and traces. Evidence for questions Metrics summarize quantities over time. Logs record events and context. Traces connect operations across a request's path. Each reveals different aspects of a failure; collecting all three without a question can still leave a system difficult to understand. Monitoring checks known conditions. Observability also supports investigating failures that were not anticipated in advance. Example: slow article search Measure request latency and error rate. Correlate a slow request with a trace through content lookup and persistence. Inspect an associated event for a failed dependency, without logging the user's entire private query history. DNS, connection establishment, application work and database work can each contribute latency. Trade-offs and privacy High-cardinality labels can make metrics expensive. Detailed logs can contain personal data or secrets. Sampling and retention reduce cost but affect the evidence available during an incident. Define user-facing reliability goals before setting alert thresholds. An alert should guide a useful response instead of merely announcing activity. Practice Instrument one operation with duration, outcome and a correlation identifier. Trigger a controlled failure and reconstruct what happened. Assessment: distinguish absence of an error log from proof of successful service. Continue with debugging, testing and CI/CD. References and verification These sources are provided for claim review. machine-learning: Machine learning Machine learning develops models whose behavior is fitted from data rather than specified entirely as explicit rules. Learning a useful pattern is different from demonstrating that the pattern generalizes. The learning problem A supervised model learns from examples paired with target values. An unsupervised method looks for structure without that same target labeling. The task determines what data, objective, and evaluation are appropriate; “AI” is not a synonym for one particular algorithm. For a sensor-quality classifier, the input might contain recent measurements and device metadata. The target records a confirmed fault. A timestamp or maintenance flag written only after the fault can accidentally reveal the answer during training. Training and evaluation Define a simple baseline before fitting a more complicated model. Separate fitting data from evaluation data, and choose a split that reflects deployment: future observations or previously unseen devices may require time-based or grouped separation. Fit preprocessing on training data and apply the fitted transformation to held-out data. Fitting normalization or feature selection on the complete dataset can leak information into evaluation. See the scikit-learn pitfalls guide. Reliability and limitations An average score can hide poor results for uncommon cases. Record errors by meaningful groups, compare costs of false positives and false negatives, and document uncertain labels. A distribution change can invalidate a previously useful model. Treat sensitive training examples as protected data. Model output still needs checks appropriate to its downstream use. Practice and progression Build a small reproducible baseline, keep the held-out examples separate, and report both its metric and three failure cases. Assessment: explain why your evaluation estimates the intended deployment behavior. Data engineering supplies dependable inputs; testing checks the surrounding system; observability helps detect changes after deployment. Continue to embeddings and recommendation systems.
embeddings: Embeddings An embedding represents an item as a vector in a space intended to preserve useful relationships for a task. Items may be words, passages, images, products, users, or other structured inputs. Representation is a modeling choice The dimensions of a learned vector generally do not have simple human-readable meanings. Nearness means similarity under a particular representation and distance function, not guaranteed factual equivalence. In a two-tower retrieval model, one model encodes the query and another encodes candidates into compatible vector spaces. A scoring operation compares the two. This is illustrated in TensorFlow Recommenders. A small similarity example For nonzero vectors, cosine similarity divides the dot product by the product of their lengths. This JavaScript example uses tiny illustrative vectors, not outputs from a trained language model: Production code also needs finite-value checks and bounds on dimensions and resource use. Some retrieval models use dot product rather than cosine; use the scoring rule the model was designed for. Common failures Vectors from incompatible models or preprocessing pipelines should not be mixed in one index without a justified transformation. Record model identity, dimensionality, input preparation, and index version. Embedding a private document does not remove its sensitivity. Apply access controls to both stored content and retrieval results. Approximate nearest-neighbor search trades exactness for efficiency and needs measurement. Exercise Write ten domain questions and manually label relevant documents. Compare retrieval results with those labels, including similar-looking but irrelevant passages. Assessment: distinguish retrieval quality from the quality of a generated answer. Continue with RAG, machine learning, and data engineering.
rag: Retrieval-augmented generation Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with a generative model. A system retrieves material relevant to an input and makes that material available during answer generation. Why retrieve before generating? A model's parameters are not a complete, current, auditable copy of your documents. Retrieval creates a path to source material that can be maintained separately. It does not guarantee that the model understands or faithfully uses that material. The original RAG paper studied a particular combination of a sequence-to-sequence generator and dense retrieval over Wikipedia. Contemporary engineering usage is broader; an arbitrary document chatbot does not necessarily implement the paper's training method. Architecture and boundaries Data engineering manages ingestion, updates, deletion, and reproducibility. Embeddings can support semantic retrieval, but keyword search or hybrid retrieval can also be suitable. A vector database is an implementation choice, not the definition of RAG. Example: asking the codex a question Suppose the question is “Does a USB connector prove that a board supports HID?” A retrieval stage should find the exact board documentation and the USB HID explanation. An answer should distinguish a physical connector, controller capabilities, and firmware support. If no exact model is known, the system should ask for that information or state the limitation. A source about one board variant is not evidence for every variant. Evaluate the stages separately Start with a fixed set of questions and expected supporting passages. Measure whether retrieval finds those passages before adding a generator. Then review answer correctness, source support, citation accuracy, and behavior when the corpus lacks an answer. Removing a document must remove its retrievable chunks as well. Track document versions and source ranges so an answer can be traced to the evidence actually used. Security and reliability Retrieved text is untrusted input. It must not override application instructions or grant permissions. Filter access before material is exposed to a model or user, and recheck policy where appropriate. Authorization applies to individual documents and derived data. Long context, stale indexes, poorly chosen chunks, and superficially similar passages can produce confident mistakes. Do not treat a displayed citation as proof that it supports the accompanying claim. Practical exercise Build a retrieval-only prototype over ten public technical documents. Save query, retrieved source IDs, source versions, and human relevance judgments. Add generation only after this baseline is understandable. Assessment: demonstrate an answerable question, an unsupported question, a stale document, and a denied document without exposing restricted content. Continue with testing, observability, and input validation.
data-engineering: Data engineering Data engineering designs and operates systems that collect, transform, store, and deliver data for dependable use. Its output is a usable data product with understood meaning, quality, ownership, and operational limits. From events to useful records A sensor reading is not useful merely because a number arrived. Consumers need its unit, timestamp convention, device identity, validity, and handling of missing or duplicate values. A schema documents structure; a data contract also explains meaning and expectations. Batch pipelines process bounded collections on a schedule or trigger. Streaming pipelines process ongoing arrivals, but still require explicit choices about ordering, late events, retries, and state. Example: a laboratory dataset Keep the original sensor events, record the schema version, and derive a table of daily measurements. When an event is repeated after a retry, use a suitable stable event identifier to avoid unintended duplication. When units change, make that transformation explicit rather than silently mixing values. ETL describes one ordering of extraction, transformation, and loading. Serialization defines the representations that ingestion and storage exchange. Quality and operations Check completeness, freshness, uniqueness, and plausible ranges according to the actual use case. A successful job exit does not establish that the delivered data is correct. Record lineage so an unexpected result can be traced to input versions and transformations. Restrict access to sensitive fields and define retention and deletion behavior across derived copies. Test replay, partial failure, and schema changes on controlled data before production use. Practice Create a small pipeline that loads timestamped observations, quarantines malformed records, and produces a summary. Run it twice against the same source and explain its duplicate behavior. Assessment: reproduce an output row from its inputs and show a freshness failure. Related skills include input validation, testing, observability, and machine learning.
etl: Extract, transform, load ETL is a data integration pattern in which data is extracted from sources, transformed into a usable representation, and loaded into a destination. ELT changes the order by loading before performing selected transformations in the destination system. Responsibilities at each stage Extraction defines what is read and how progress is tracked. Transformation defines mapping, cleaning, normalization, and derived values. Loading defines how destination records are inserted, replaced, or merged. Neither acronym specifies a universal tool, schedule, or consistency guarantee. Data engineering supplies the broader operational design. A measurement example A source contains a device ID, an event timestamp, a temperature, and its unit. Extract the original rows, validate the contract, convert supported units into the documented target unit, and load the result with the original event ID. Do not convert missing readings to zero. Quarantine unknown units with an explanation. Keep the source representation so an incorrect transformation can be repaired and replayed. Failure and recovery An interruption can occur after some rows are written but before the job records success. Design retry behavior deliberately: stable keys, transactional boundaries, checkpoints, or staging tables may be appropriate. A checkpoint is only useful when its relationship to committed output is understood. Source changes during extraction can create an inconsistent view. Decide whether a snapshot, change log, watermark, or other mechanism meets the use case rather than assuming one read sees everything at one instant. Exercise Import a small CSV-like source into a test table. Include a duplicate event, a bad timestamp, and an unsupported unit. Rerun after a simulated interruption and reconcile source, accepted, rejected, and destination counts. Assessment: explain every missing or repeated row. Continue with serialization, input validation, and testing.
serialization: Serialization and file formats Serialization maps structured values into a representation that can be stored or transmitted. Deserialization interprets that representation to recover values according to a format and schema. Extension, format, and encoding A filename extension is a naming convention. A .dat file may contain text, packed binary records, or an application-specific format; the extension does not establish its layout. Renaming a file does not convert its contents. Text encoding maps characters to bytes. A format describes how values are organized. A schema adds constraints and meaning, such as which fields are required and which unit a number represents. A small JSON example Successful parsing does not validate an application contract. Check required fields, supported units, numeric limits, and resource bounds before using the result. JSON does not preserve arbitrary language-specific objects, functions, or object identity. Binary formats A fixed-width binary record requires agreement on field sizes, byte order, signedness, and alignment. Changing one of those assumptions can produce plausible but incorrect numbers. Preserve a format version and test against known byte sequences. Serialization is different from compression and encryption. A binary representation is not automatically secret. Some deserialization mechanisms can construct executable objects; choose a format and parser suitable for untrusted input. Exercise Document a sensor-message schema and round-trip several valid examples. Reject malformed text, missing fields, and oversized input. Assessment: explain what parsing guarantees and what input validation must still check. Connect this to UART, MQTT, and ETL.
recommendation-systems: Recommendation systems A recommendation system selects and orders items for a user or context using an explicit objective and available evidence. Its behavior depends on data, candidate selection, scoring, constraints, and feedback. Retrieval and ranking Candidate retrieval narrows a large collection to a tractable set. Ranking then scores or orders those candidates for the current request. A further stage can apply eligibility, diversity, or product constraints. This division is illustrated by the TensorFlow retrieval tutorial. Content-based approaches use item characteristics. Collaborative approaches learn from patterns across interactions. Embeddings can represent users or items for similarity-based retrieval, but a system need not use a neural model to recommend useful material. Example: next topics in the codex A transparent baseline recommends documented prerequisites that a learner has not completed. It can then suggest a connected concept relevant to a chosen engineering role. This uses the knowledge graph and explicit learning state rather than inferring ability from clicks alone. Compare that baseline with a learned ranker only when there is enough appropriate data and a meaningful evaluation objective. Feedback is imperfect evidence A click can mean curiosity, confusion, or accidental selection. More engagement does not necessarily mean more learning or satisfaction. Exposure also affects which feedback is observed: unseen items cannot receive the same interaction opportunities. Avoid treating a vendor's illustrative system description as disclosure of its complete current implementation. Research claims about social-media behavior and legal disputes remain in the original archive pending separate verification. Practice Build a small recommendation list with an explanation for every item. Compare relevance, coverage, and duplicate content against a simple chronological baseline. Assessment: describe cold-start behavior and one feedback loop that could narrow recommendations. Related concepts include machine learning, data engineering, and testing.
